text: In a series from Grenoble, 50 epilepsy patients heard something when they were stimulated through depth electrodes. Most of what they heard was a simple sound, or a change in the sounds already in the room. A few of the reports were of music or of speaking voices.
A 2010 review of 93 reports lists voices and music among the effects reported from the superior temporal gyrus. It records what has been reported at least once and gives no frequencies.

In a series of 28 epilepsy patients, stimulation of the auditory cortex produced sound at 113 sites. At three of them the patient heard familiar music or songs. The count of three was read in the preprint of the paper.
A 2019 systematic review of musical hallucinations in epilepsy cites only Penfield and Perot 1963 for music produced by stimulation inside the skull.

Recording, not stimulation. Brain activity was recorded from 29 epilepsy patients while they listened to Pink Floyd’s “Another Brick in the Wall, Part 1”, and a recognisable version of the song was rebuilt from the recordings. The superior temporal gyrus carried most of the information, the right side more than the left.

In one man of 45 with electrodes over the right fusiform gyrus, stimulating two face-selective spots made the faces of the people in the room look distorted. Objects in the room were not affected in the same way, and nothing happened with sham stimulation.

In one man of 22 with epilepsy, stimulating a scene-selective area on the underside of the right temporal lobe made him see places, among them a train station and a street in his own neighbourhood. Not every scene returned when the same site was stimulated again.

A review of 80 years of reports found 273 stimulations that brought back a memory, from 73 published patients and 18 of the reviewers’ own. Most of the memories were vague. About 14% were of one particular event in the patient’s life. Nearly all came from the temporal lobe, and well under 1% of stimulations produced one.

Of 29 patients with temporal lobe epilepsy studied with depth electrodes, 18 had dream-like experiences such as flash-backs, feelings of familiarity, hallucinations or sudden emotions, in seizures or under stimulation. These came only when the seizure or the current reached the limbic structures deep in the lobe. The outer temporal cortex did not have to be involved.

An earlier study gave 3,495 stimulations to deep structures of the temporal lobe in 36 patients and recorded 267 mental responses. Its authors tied the kind of experience more to the person than to the exact spot stimulated. These figures are as given by the 2017 review. The study itself was not read for this page.

In 16 patients with temporal lobe epilepsy, stimulation set off a dreamy state, meaning déjà vu or vivid scenes like memories, 43 times in 14 of them. It could be started from the amygdala, from the front of the hippocampus or from the outer temporal cortex, and a larger share of the deep sites than of the outer sites produced it.

In 24 patients and 280 stimulations, déjà vu was linked mainly to the entorhinal cortex, and the recall of past scenes to the perirhinal cortex. These are two strips of cortex beside the hippocampus. Both effects were uncommon.

Loftus and Loftus noted that only 40 of Penfield’s 1,132 patients gave such responses. From Penfield and Perot’s own case notes they argued that even the most lifelike reports read as scenes the patient put together, and not as the replay of a stored record.

Sjöberg argues that a memory reported under stimulation may be a mental event which the patient, steered by the current and by the surgeon’s questions, takes for a real memory. He notes that such reports have not come from modern awake surgery for tumours, and says that neither account can yet be proved.

In 1959 Penfield offered “interpretive cortex” as a working name for parts of both temporal lobes where a gentle current sometimes gave one of two responses: a vivid return of a past experience, or a sudden change in how the present felt.
In a lecture of 1957 Penfield listed the feelings that stimulation could produce as fear, loneliness, separation, sorrow and disgust. He gave no counts.

In 74 epilepsy patients, 79 of 938 stimulations of the temporal lobe produced an emotion, and in 67 of the 79 it was fear. Fear came most often from the amygdala, and women reported it more often than men.

In eight epilepsy patients, about half of the brief stimulations of the amygdala changed how the patient felt. On the right the feeling was always unpleasant: fear, anxiety or sadness. On the left it was unpleasant about half the time and happy the rest. Five of the eight had an electrode on the right and five on the left.

In nine epilepsy patients, stimulating the amygdala reliably changed sweating and heart rate, and seven of the nine felt no emotion. One man felt fear that grew to terror as the voltage on his right amygdala was raised.

In 10 epilepsy patients, stimulating the pregenual anterior cingulate cortex, the part in front of the corpus callosum, made them laugh. In half of them the laughter came with a feeling of amusement. In the other half amusement was not evident. The ten are the patients who laughed, out of a larger group that was stimulated.

In a woman of 23 with epilepsy, stimulating the cingulum bundle on the left produced smiling, laughter and a calm, happy mood. Her surgeons then used it to keep her calm through brain surgery done while she was awake. Two further patients showed the same smiling and lift of mood. Grey matter nearby gave nothing in the first patient.
In one patient, stimulation of a small area at the front of the supplementary motor area, on the left, produced laughter.

In three epilepsy patients whose seizures began with a feeling of bliss, a few seconds of stimulation of the upper front part of the insula brought on the same state. The site was on the right in two and on the left in one. Stimulation of other sites did not do it.
A man of 51 who did not have such seizures reported bliss and mental clarity when the same part of the left insula was stimulated. Five other patients tested in similar conditions did not.

An earlier letter from the same group reported a woman of 23 whose seizures began with a feeling of bliss, in whom three seconds of stimulation of the same region brought the feeling on. The letter was not read for this page. This account is from the group’s later papers.

In a study of 25 epilepsy patients with electrodes already in place, 100 to 200 seconds of stimulation of the lateral orbitofrontal cortex on one side lifted mood in those with moderate to severe symptoms of depression, more so at the higher current. Patients with few or no such symptoms showed no significant change. The effect was measured over minutes.

In six people whose depression had not responded to other treatment, continuous stimulation of the white matter beside the subgenual cingulate was followed by a lasting response in four at six months. In the operating room patients reported a sudden calm or lightness, and a room that looked brighter, when the current was on. They reported nothing with sham stimulation. The trial had no placebo group.

In one woman of 36 with severe depression of long standing, doctors found a signal in her amygdala that tracked her worst symptoms. They implanted a device that answered the signal with six seconds of stimulation to the right ventral capsule and ventral striatum. Her depression score fell from 33 to 14 in 12 days and later fell below 10, the level counted as remission. There was no control condition.

A man of about 60 was treated for severe obsessive-compulsive disorder by deep brain stimulation of the nucleus accumbens. He had never cared much for music. About six months after surgery he became a devoted listener to Johnny Cash, after hearing one of his songs by chance. When the stimulator’s batteries ran down he went back to his old favourites. The change came together with a large improvement in his illness and in his confidence.

In two men with epilepsy, stimulating the anterior midcingulate cortex produced a faster heartbeat, a sensation in the chest or neck, and a feeling that a challenge was coming, with a determination to get through it. The feeling included worry. Neither man reported anything in sham trials.

In a woman of 43 being assessed for epilepsy surgery, stimulating the right angular gyrus first made her feel that she was sinking into the bed or falling. At a slightly higher current she reported seeing herself from above, lying in bed, and this happened three times. She saw only her legs and lower trunk.

The 1937 figure rested on 126 usable operation records out of 163 operations done under local anaesthesia from 1928 to 1936. Boldrey compiled 170 summary charts, one for each movement or sensation. The 1950 figures drew on about 400 craniotomies, including a second series from 1936 to 1947.

Hortense Pauline Cantlie drew the homunculus. One combined figure appeared in the 1937 paper. For the 1950 book she drew two new figures, one sensory (Fig. 17) and one motor (Fig. 22). In the reproductions viewed, both drawings carry her monogram and the year 1948.

Penfield and Rasmussen wrote that the motor homunculus may be used as an aid to memory and called it “a cartoon of representation in which scientific accuracy is impossible” (p. 56). Of the sensory homunculus they wrote that such drawings become confusing if too much significance is attributed to shape and comparative size, and that the indication of extent under the figure corrects this (p. 214).

Every body-part label on the 1950 plates except Gen. has a block line along the cortex. The three function words on the motor figure are brackets and have no line. The legend of the sensory figure says the length of these lines shows the comparative extent of each representation more accurately than the drawing. Wright (1956) measured every line, 28 on the sensory figure and 22 on the motor figure. The legend of the motor figure does not repeat the statement.

Penfield and Boldrey scaled the 1937 figure by the vertical extent of each part along the central sulcus, without statistics. A 2017 reanalysis found that the figure was not in proportion to the paper’s own measurements. Stimulus intensity, number of patients, number of stimulations per patient and overlap between parts were not taken into account. The reanalysed sensory maps overlap substantially, mostly near the central sulcus.

The 1937 figure was a single drawing without labels, not laid on the brain. The 1950 figures are each laid on the outline of a coronal section, with named labels and block lines. The sensory figure adds the genitals and an intra-abdominal field. The motor figure adds three function brackets.

Penfield’s patients were awake. Each response was dictated to a stenographer and tied to a numbered ticket on the cortex. In one 1937 case the record includes tingling in the little finger, numbness in the shoulder, a shock-like feeling in four fingers that spared the thumb, and a feeling that the thumb moved when it did not.

In a series of 50 patients mapped from 2008 to 2016, 258 of 647 sites on the crown of the postcentral gyrus gave a sensation (40%), at a mean threshold of 2.67 mA. Tingling was almost the only sensation. One patient reported pain, one a bad taste and one burning in the hand. No patient reported a sense of movement.
According to the 2018 authors, Penfield found 25% of sensory responses outside the postcentral gyrus. Their own series found none at 1,025 sites stimulated outside it.

Primary somatosensory cortex comprises four cytoarchitectonic areas. Area 3a lies in the fundus of the central sulcus and area 3b on its posterior bank. Area 1 lies on the crown of the postcentral gyrus and extends into the postcentral sulcus. Area 2 lies mainly on the anterior bank of the postcentral sulcus. The borders vary between brains.

Surface stimulation in the 2018 series reached only area 1 on the gyral crown. Depth-electrode stimulation in 20 patients (149 positive sites of 177, most in sulcal cortex) found a gross medial-to-lateral order across all of primary somatosensory cortex that was consistent with the classical homunculus.
Penfield wrote that when he made a conscious patient move his hand by stimulating the motor cortex and asked him about it, the reply was invariably: “I didn’t do that. You did.” (p. 76).

In a series of 100 patients published in 2020, the Results report 248 positive sites among 608 precentral sites stimulated. The abstract says 245 of the 248 lay in the precentral gyrus. The mean threshold was 2.1 mA. Movements were basic and stereotyped, and were fast without the profile of a natural movement. Flexions of the wrist and digits were far more frequent than extensions. No complex action, such as bringing food to the mouth, was seen.

Responses in the 2020 series were judged from the patient’s report and the team’s observation, without EMG. 59% of precentral sites gave no response, and the part of area 4 buried in the central sulcus could not be reached.

Focal motor seizures can spread through neighbouring body parts in the order of the motor map. This is the Jacksonian march. Bravais described such seizures in 1827. Hughlings Jackson described the march between 1868 and 1870 and inferred that body parts are represented in separate parts of the brain. Penfield and Boldrey published their stimulation map in 1937. A 2024 series found that spread is not explained by adjacency alone.

According to the 2020 authors, Penfield found about 20% of motor responses outside the precentral gyrus, particularly in the postcentral gyrus. In their own series, 3 of 1,937 sites stimulated outside the precentral gyrus produced movement.

A commentary on the 2020 data describes, for the upper limb and the head, a gradual progression with overlap between neighbouring parts, and no discrete zones of the kind drawn in 1950. The study’s authors use the term relative somatotopy for the elbow, wrist and hand region.

Primary motor cortex (area 4) lies mostly in the anterior bank of the central sulcus. Near the midline it widens onto the gyral surface and the paracentral lobule. Much of the exposed crown of the precentral gyrus is premotor cortex (area 6).

Precision fMRI in 7 intensively scanned adults, replicated in group-averaged datasets of about 4,000, 3,928 and 812 people, divides the precentral gyrus into three effector regions (foot, hand, mouth) that alternate with three inter-effector regions. See column C of Fig. 2.

Single-neuron recordings from 20 microelectrode arrays in 8 people found the whole body represented at every sampled site on the crown of the precentral gyrus, with relative strength roughly following the homunculus.
Lower-limb sites were rare in the 2018 series: one for the feet, two for the leg, one for the knee, three for the thigh and one for the hip, out of 258 positive sites.

Infarcts in the territory of the anterior cerebral artery, which supplies the medial frontal lobe and the medial motor and sensory cortex, typically cause weakness that is greatest in the opposite leg, with the arm and face typically spared. Sensory loss is less common. In one series of 51 patients, 86% had a motor deficit of the leg and 29% a sensory deficit.
Lower-limb movements were evoked at 10 sites in 7 patients in the 2020 series (foot 4, knee 1, hip 4, buttock 1), all in the right hemisphere. The supplementary motor area was not stimulated.
In the foot effector region the toes are central, with ankle, knee and hip in zones around them (task fMRI in 2 participants). The 1950 figure draws the same parts in a line.
The 2018 series found one abdomen site and three thorax sites, in four patients.
In the 2017 reanalysis of the 1937 motor data, too few trunk stimulations were recorded for an area or a length to be measured.
Isometric contraction of the abdominal muscles co-activated the inter-effector regions and the cingulo-opercular network (2 participants).

fMRI during isometric head rotation in 17 healthy adults found two foci in the precentral gyrus, one medial and anterior to the hand knob and one lateral and ventral to it. The authors suggest the medial focus has the larger role in head movement. That fits earlier studies which place the neck between the trunk and arm representations, as in the sensory figure. The study did not map the shoulder or the trunk. Activation was bilateral with contralateral predominance.

The 2015 authors note that Penfield’s head-movement results came from only nine patients and were not consistent, against more than 200 patients for limb movements. The 1950 text says that neck movement on the strip is small, is usually head retraction, and does not match the position of neck sensation (p. 57).
Depth-electrode stimulation of sulcal cortex found a forehead representation that the authors describe as previously unreported.
On the hairy skin of the upper limb, spatial acuity for touch improves from the shoulder to the back of the hand. Spatial acuity for pain runs the opposite way.

Depth-electrode stimulation of sulcal cortex evoked sensations referred to the deep elbow and wrist joints, which the authors describe as previously unreported. Surface stimulation in the 2018 series had found elbow and wrist skin sites.
In a man with tetraplegia, microstimulation of left primary somatosensory cortex evoked both cutaneous and proprioceptive sensations in the right arm, mostly the upper arm and forearm.

Infarcts in the territory of the middle cerebral artery, which supplies most of the lateral surface, typically cause weakness that is worse in the opposite arm and face than in the leg. Sensory loss mainly affects the face and arm. Occlusion of the main stem causes weakness of the whole side.
In the 2020 series shoulder movements lay medially and hand movements laterally. Each overlapped considerably with the elbow and wrist representations between them.

Activation peaks for shoulder, elbow and wrist are arranged concentrically around the hand peak (2 participants). The 1950 figure draws them in a line. The hand task was closing the whole hand, so single digits were not tested.

Finger sites ran in order from little finger (medial) to thumb (lateral) and together spanned about 1.5 cm of the gyral crown. Mean thresholds were 2.39 mA for finger sites and 2.60 mA for tongue sites. These two did not differ significantly, and both were lower than for other body parts (mean 3.5 mA).

Across 11 body sites tested in 26 healthy volunteers in two experiments, the fingertip had the finest spatial acuity for both touch and pain. Read from the paper’s bar chart, two touches were told apart at roughly 0.3 cm on the fingertip and at roughly 2 to 3 cm on the shoulder. The paper prints no table of thresholds, so these values are approximate.

In nine string players, magnetic responses to touch on the left thumb and little finger were stronger and shifted compared with six controls, which the authors read as a larger cortical representation of the left-hand digits. The effect was smaller for the thumb than for the little finger, absent for the right hand, and greater in those who had started playing younger. Only those two digits were tested.

In four blind Braille teachers who read with three fingers of each hand, finger topography was disordered in at least one hemisphere in every reader, and all four tended to misjudge which finger had been touched. Blind one-finger readers did not differ from sighted controls.
In one arm amputee, stimuli applied to the lower face, or 7 cm above the stump, evoked precisely localised sensations in individual phantom digits.

Three adults were scanned twice before arm amputation and at 3 and 6 months afterwards. One was scanned again at 18 months and one at five years. Hand and lip maps in primary somatosensory cortex stayed stable, and the result was replicated in primary motor cortex. A classifier trained on finger-movement activity before surgery distinguished attempted phantom finger movements above the 50% chance level at every later scan. At each participant’s last scan its accuracy was 90%, 67% and 89%. The maps were evoked by movement, not touch.

An older account held that after amputation the neighbouring face map takes over the hand territory. In 13 arm amputees studied with MEG, the shift of the lip representation toward the hand area correlated with phantom pain intensity (r = 0.93).

A 2013 study of 18 arm amputees instead linked worse phantom pain to more activity and more grey matter in the former hand area, and to weaker resting-state connectivity between that area and the hand area of the opposite hemisphere.

Microstimulation through electrode arrays in area 1 of the hand region evoked touch sensations that a man with long-standing spinal cord injury felt as coming from his own hand. Raising the current raised the perceived intensity. By the first author’s dissertation, the sensations lay at the bases of the index to little fingers on the palm side, with none on the thumb or on a fingertip.

A man with spinal cord injury controlled a robotic arm through a brain implant. With touch feedback added by microstimulation of the hand region of his sensory cortex, his median time for a successful trial on a clinical arm-function test was 10.2 s, against 20.9 s without it.

Hand and wrist responses in 51 patients suggested a medial wrist cluster, a central all-fingers cluster and a lateral individual-finger cluster (mean |x| 26.2, 32.9 and 35.4 mm). Thumb flexion made up half of single-finger responses.
Finger flexion was evoked 63 times and finger extension 8 times in the 2020 series.

The little-finger-to-thumb sequence drawn in 1950 is absent from the 2020 group data. Of the three patients with separate thumb and other single-digit sites, only one showed the thumb lateral and the other digits in order medially.

The motor hand area most often lies in a knob of the precentral gyrus that looks like an omega or epsilon in axial images and like a hook in sagittal images. The knob is a reliable landmark for finding the precentral gyrus in normal and diseased brains.

A 96-electrode array in the arm and hand area of primary motor cortex, as the authors describe the site, let a man with tetraplegia move a cursor, open simulated e-mail and open and close a prosthetic hand, three years after spinal cord injury.

Two arrays in the hand knob area of the precentral gyrus, which the authors call a premotor area, decoded the attempted handwriting of a man with a paralysed hand at 90 characters per minute, with 94.1% raw accuracy.

The 2018 series ordered the face, tongue excluded, from medial to lateral: eyebrows, eyes, cheeks, both lips, teeth, gums, jaws, pharynx, larynx. The order rests on few sites, one each for eyebrows, eyes, nose, face, gums and pharynx. In the paper’s own table the teeth sites lie below the gums and jaw sites.

Penfield and Boldrey wrote in 1937 that responses were too few to fix the sequence position of the nose, the neck and taste, and that eye turning was left out of their chart. Catani (2017) reads this as an admission that the face representation may mislead.
According to the 2018 authors, 13% of face and tongue sensory responses in Penfield’s work (27 of 202) were felt on both sides. Their own series recorded none.
An MEG study found same-side activation of primary somatosensory cortex after touch to the upper lip in 69% of cases, to the lower lip in 85% and to the tongue in 88%.

Face movements, tongue included, were evoked in 52 patients. The authors describe a medial-to-lateral sequence of forehead, eyebrows, eyes, nose, cheeks, both lips and chin. Responses above the lips were few (forehead 2, eyebrow 1, eyelid 2, nostril 1, cheek 11).
In one 1937 case the patient said he could not help closing his right eye. He closed both.
Raising the eyebrows co-activated the inter-effector regions and the cingulo-opercular network (2 participants).
In the 2023 task data (2 participants), eyelid movement was the preferred movement at the centre of one inter-effector region.
In 14 patients tongue sites ran from tip (medial) to base (lateral). The tongue spanned about 2.5 cm of the gyral crown, against about 1.5 cm for the five fingers together.

In one 1937 case, one point gave numbness on the right side of the tongue, a neighbouring point gave tingling on the right side, more at the tip, and another point gave numbness at the midline of the back of the tongue.
Catani (2017) judges the tongue exaggerated in the 1937 figure and corrected in the 1950 figures.
The 2020 series counted 38 lip, 35 tongue and 12 jaw responses. In the 11 patients with both lip and tongue sites, the order from medial to lateral was upper lip, lower lip, tongue.

According to the 2020 authors, Penfield described vocalization, salivation and mastication from the lips, jaw and tongue zone. None of the three was seen in their series. The 1950 text says that vocalization has no fixed place in the sequence and that salivation was more often a postcentral than a precentral response.
The 1937 text reports 21 motor stimulations for mouth and lips, 18 precentral and 3 postcentral. Catani counts 64 plotted points for the same parts in the paper’s Fig. 7.
In the mouth effector region the tongue is central and the jaw more peripheral, with the larynx at the perimeter. The paper’s schematic also draws the eyes at the outer edge of this region.

Arrays in area 6v (ventral premotor cortex, on the ventral precentral gyrus) decoded the attempted speech of a woman with ALS at 62 words per minute. Two further arrays in area 44 carried almost no speech information.
A surface electrode grid over the sensorimotor and temporal speech cortex of a woman paralysed by a brainstem stroke decoded text at a median of 78 words per minute.
In one 1937 case the patient made a small noise during stimulation, recorded as vocalisation, and said he could not help it. Upper and lower lips moved equally on both sides.
The 2020 series recorded 14 larynx responses at the lateral end of the strip (barycentre |x| 60.2, z 14.0 mm). No vocalization was observed. The motor figure has no larynx label.

fMRI during vocalization shows two larynx representations, a dorsal and a ventral one. The dorsal one lies in primary motor cortex. The ventral one does not, and the authors speculate that it lies in premotor cortex.
In the 2023 task data (2 participants), swallowing was the preferred movement at the centre of one inter-effector region.

The 1950 text says that the position of the genitalia relative to the toes is not clear and may be posterior to the toes (p. 45). The legend of the 1937 figure says that genitalia and rectum are not figured.

According to Kell et al. (2005), repeated by Cazala et al. (2015), Penfield and Rasmussen obtained genital sensation in three of 400 patients, from cortex beside the central fissure 1 cm behind the upper-leg and lower-trunk representation, and none from the medial surface of the postcentral gyrus. That passage of the 1950 book was not read for this build.

Other accounts of Penfield’s evidence differ. Di Noto et al. (2013) say the 1950 book covers 400 operations, at least 9 of them on women, and that the medial placement of the female genitals rests on one patient. Proelss et al. (2025) say that Penfield’s maps showed no genital responses in the dorsal postcentral gyrus. Penfield reported little about the women he mapped, and the figure is drawn as male.

In 8 men, brushing of the penis activated the contralateral postcentral gyrus about 1 cm lateral to the big toe (group foci at Talairach 24, −33, 72 for the prepuce and 24, −35, 68 for the shaft). The lower abdominal wall, tested in 4 of the men, overlapped the penile focus with its centre slightly more lateral. The authors found no sign of a penile representation on the medial wall.
In 13 men scanned at 7 tesla, brushing of the penile shaft activated primary somatosensory cortex dorsolateral to the foot. The authors assign a deeper midline activation to midcingulate cortex.

In 20 women, an oscillating membrane on the clitoral region, contrasted with the hand, activated the dorsolateral postcentral gyrus (both hemispheres in 16, one in 4), where the authors place it beside the hip and upper leg. The peak varied considerably between individuals.

In awake surgery on 8 tumour patients, all 3 men reported genital sensations from the dorsal postcentral gyrus, beside the upper leg and thigh, extending into the adjacent sulcus in two. None of the 5 women did. At the fMRI-defined female genital site they often reported leg sensations. Stimulation current was fixed, so a higher threshold in women is not excluded.
The 2018 series of 50 patients does not mention genital sensations.

Other studies point to the medial wall. In 11 women, self-stimulation of the clitoris, vagina and cervix activated the paracentral lobule (Komisaruk et al. 2011, no coordinates published). The 2015 review notes that these responses may lie in motor cortex. A 2010 perfusion study in 16 men reported both a paracentral and a lateral postcentral focus (Georgiadis et al. 2010, as tabulated in the review). Both foci are correlations of blood flow with penile circumference or its rate of change, not responses to touch alone.

Evoked potentials to pudendal nerve stimulation were recorded from the mesial surface, in front of the foot area, in epilepsy patients (Allison et al. 1996). The 2015 review tentatively accepts two representations, one medial and one lateral.

In the women of the 2022 study with a mapped left-hemisphere genital field (18 of 20 by the paper’s table), cortical thickness of that field correlated with self-reported intercourse frequency over the previous 12 months (partial r = 0.701). The design is cross-sectional and does not show direction of effect. A 2026 study by the same group recruited 128 women, 64 of them exposed to childhood sexual abuse. Its left-hemisphere analyses included at most 89 women. It found no association between field thickness and sexual frequency over the previous 12 months, in the whole sample or in either group.
The 2018 series found one pharynx site and two larynx sites, at the lateral end of the sequence.
The 2018 series does not mention intra-abdominal or visceral sensations. Abdomen appears there only as a skin site.

The evidence is precision resting-state fMRI in 7 adults (172 to 1,813 minutes of resting data each). A movement task battery and a planning task were run in 2 of them, a foot, hand and tongue localiser in 3, and a larynx task in 3 adults, one of whom was not among the 7. The resting-state pattern was replicated in group-averaged data from UK Biobank (about 4,000), ABCD (3,928) and the Human Connectome Project (812). The authors caution that their schematic is not a precise map.

Inter-effector cortex is thinner than effector cortex. The three regions are strongly connected to each other and to the cingulo-opercular network, the dorsolateral putamen and the centromedian nucleus of the thalamus.

They show weak movement specificity. In a task with separate planning and execution phases for hand and foot movements, run in 2 participants, they were more active during planning than during execution. The effector regions were not.

In the task data, abdominal movement, eyelid movement and swallowing were the preferred movements at the centres of the three inter-effector regions. The paper lists them in that order and does not state the pairing with superior, middle and inferior in a sentence.

Lies between the foot and hand effector regions. Gordon et al. cite depth-electrode recordings (Jensen et al. 2023) as showing that this region is active during foot, hand and mouth movements. The recording study, in 13 patients, places its main shared site deep in the central sulcus at its mid-lateral part, active during hand, tongue and foot movements. Its authors say only that the superior region of Gordon et al. may overlie a secondary site, which they saw in five patients.

Lies between the hand and mouth effector regions. The authors mapped the published movement sites from surface stimulation in 100 patients (Roux et al. 2020) onto a group surface and found none in a zone corresponding to this region. Sites that gave no movement were not part of that analysis.

Last in the sequence, below the mouth effector region and just above the lateral sulcus. Its position is shown by the sixth seed in the paper’s first figure and by the positions in its Supplementary Table 1.

Each effector region is drawn as concentric zones, with the distal part (toes, fingers, tongue) at the centre and proximal parts (knee, shoulder, larynx) on the perimeter. The hand task was closing the whole hand. Fingers were not tested one by one.
The authors note that Penfield’s stimulation elicited movement from about half of sites, mostly of the foot, hand and mouth, and that sites giving no movement were historically not recorded.
